title: Modeling the Relationship Between Psychosocial Stressor Exposure and Safety Compliance in a Developing Economy Construction Industry
content: Psychosocial hazards are established antecedents of psychological strain among construction personnel, yet whether that strain transmits exposure to in-role safety behavior has rarely been tested against criteria capable of detecting construct redundancy. This study examined the sequence linking psychosocial stressor exposure and role and employment insecurity to safety compliance through perceived strain-related safety impairment among construction personnel. A questionnaire survey obtained 196 responses, of which 157 were retained after removal of unengaged and duplicate cases. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was applied, with discriminant validity assessed by the heterotrait-monotrait ratio, mediation evaluated through specific indirect effects, and predictive relevance established out of sample against naive and linear benchmarks. Two construct pairs proved indistinguishable before remediation, one at unity. Exposure predicted impairment (0.676) and compliance (−0.301), whereas impairment predicted compliance non-significantly, and the indirect effect spanned zero. Insecurity predicted compliance positively (0.600), contrary to expectation. The findings indicate that psychosocial exposure reaches enforced safety behavior without an intervening deterioration in perceived functioning, directing preventive effort toward the organization of work rather than individual psychological capacity, and demonstrating that reported construct separations in this literature warrant re-examination under sensitive criteria.
